Short questions on bisulfite chemistry, alignment, QC and the alternatives. Try each on paper first, then open the answer.

---

**Q1.** What do C, 5mC, 5hmC and 5caC read as after bisulfite treatment and PCR? What does that mean for "methylation" measured by WGBS?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
C → T; 5mC → C; 5hmC → C (it forms a stable sulfonate adduct, CMS); 5caC (and 5fC) → T. WGBS therefore measures **5mC + 5hmC** together; in tissues with much 5hmC (brain) "methylation" is partly 5hmC.
:::

---

**Q2.** The top strand of a genomic segment is 5'-TCGACA-3' and its CpG is methylated. Write the OT read after bisulfite conversion.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
Only the C of the CpG is protected.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
5'-**TCGATA**-3': the C in CG stays C, the C in CA becomes T.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why can bisulfite reads not be aligned well with a normal aligner, and how does Bismark solve it?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every unmethylated C appears as a T, so reads carry many C/T mismatches that depend on methylation (biasing alignment against unmethylated reads), and the reads are low-complexity. Bismark converts all Cs to Ts in the read, aligns it with bowtie2 to a C→T and a G→A converted genome, keeps reads with a unique best hit, and then compares the original read with the original genome to call methylation.
:::

---

**Q4.** In a directional WGBS library, from which strands does read 1 come? What happens if you align a non-directional (PBAT) library in directional mode?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Read 1 comes from the original top (OT) or original bottom (OB) strand. A non-directional library also contains reads from CTOT and CTOB; in directional mode those are not tried, so roughly half of the reads fail to align.
:::

---

**Q5.** A mammalian WGBS library has 0.8% methylated CHH calls. What is the conversion rate, and what β would a truly unmethylated CpG show? When would this estimate be wrong?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Conversion 99.2%; an unmethylated CpG shows β ≈ 0.008. The estimate is wrong where non-CpG methylation is real (neurons, embryonic stem cells, plants); there use an unmethylated spike-in such as lambda DNA.
:::

---

**Q6.** An M-bias plot of read 2 shows 40% CpG methylation at positions 1–3 and a flat 70% after position 5. Read 1 is flat at 70%. What causes this and what do you do?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
End repair before adapter ligation fills the fragment ends with unmethylated C; read 2 starts in that filled-in DNA, so its first bases look unmethylated. Ignore the first ~4–5 positions of read 2 when extracting calls (`--ignore_r2 5`), then check the plot again. Do not discard the reads.
:::

---

**Q7.** A CpG has 6 methylated reads out of 8. Another has 60 of 80. Give β and an approximate 95% interval for each.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Both β = 0.75. SE = $\sqrt{0.75 \cdot 0.25/N}$: 0.153 for 8 reads (interval about 0.45–1.0; the exact binomial interval is 0.35–0.97), 0.048 for 80 reads (0.65–0.85). Ten times more reads, about three times narrower.
:::

---

**Q8.** Should you remove PCR duplicates from (a) a WGBS library and (b) an RRBS library? Explain.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
(a) Yes: reads with the same start and strand are likely copies of one molecule and would be counted as independent observations, inflating confidence. (b) No: RRBS fragments all start at MspI sites, so identical starts are expected; deduplication would discard most of the data.
:::

---

**Q9.** In GM12878, CpGs where the cell line is homozygous for a C>T SNP show β ≈ 0.01 in Bismark output. Explain, and say how such sites can be detected from the bisulfite data themselves.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
There is no C at the site, so every read has T, exactly what an unmethylated C gives: the pipeline reports an unmethylated CpG that does not exist. Reads from the opposite strand show A instead of G at the paired position, which bisulfite cannot cause; SNP-aware callers (Bis-SNP, BISCUIT, gemBS) use this to call the genotype. Otherwise, filter CpGs that overlap known SNPs.
:::

---

**Q10.** Give one advantage of EM-seq and one of TAPS over bisulfite sequencing.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
EM-seq: much less DNA damage, so it works from very little input (cell-free DNA) with more even coverage, and it gives the same readout as bisulfite so the same pipeline works. TAPS: only modified cytosines change (to T), so reads keep four letters, align better and waste less sequencing; variants separate 5mC from 5hmC.
:::
